title: The Derring Effect Deliberate Errors Enhance Learning https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2Fxge0001072
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 26, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page covers Wong and Lim's research on the derring effect, a counterintuitive finding that deliberately making and then correcting an error enhances learning even when the learner already knows the correct answer. Across three experiments, deliberate erring outperformed traditional errorless strategies like copying or generating the correct answer directly. The researchers explore possible mechanisms, including enhanced processing of the target information during correction and the role of elaboration, and note that participants consistently underestimated how effective this error-based approach actually was. Barton's summary frames the practical opportunity as guiding students to deliberately commit and correct conceptually plausible but inaccurate responses, which can double as a discussion prompt as well as a learning technique. It also flags a metacognitive angle: because students underrate deliberate erring's value, teachers need to explicitly teach the technique rather than assume students will adopt it on their own.
points: Deliberately making and then correcting an error, even when the learner already knows the right answer, outperforms traditional errorless learning strategies like copying or generating the correct answer directly.
Students consistently underestimate how effective deliberate erring is, so teachers need to explicitly explain and teach the technique rather than assume it will be adopted naturally.
Deliberate erring works best when the error is conceptually plausible rather than random, since a plausible wrong answer can also stimulate meaningful class discussion.
This approach can be built directly into homework and classroom activities, helping students surface and address gaps in their understanding proactively rather than after a test.
quotes: This research article investigates the derring effect, a counterintuitive phenomenon where deliberately making and correcting errors enhances learning, even when the correct answer is known.
Three experiments demonstrate that this method surpasses traditional errorless learning strategies, such as copying or generating correct answers.
Interestingly, participants consistently underestimated the effectiveness of this error-based approach.

Teachers can guide students to intentionally make and then correct plausible but inaccurate responses. This approach can help students identify gaps in their understanding and turn mistakes into learning experiences.
Our findings suggest that preventing errors in low-stakes learning contexts may, in itself, be an error.
